Parable of the Two Great Eagles, and the Cropping of the Cedar of Lebanon. Judah Is to Be Judged for Revolting from Babylon, Which Had Set Up Zedekiah instead of Jehoiachin, to Egypt; God Himself, as the Rival of the Babylonian King, Is to Plant the Gospel Cedar of Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen20343" type="x-p"/> The date of the prophecy is between the sixth month of Zedekiah's sixth year of reign and the fifth month of the seventh year after the carrying away of Jehoiachin, that is, five years before the destruction of Jerusalem [Henderson].<div eID="gen20343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11264"/><hi type="bold">2. riddle--</hi>a continued allegory, expressed enigmatically, requiring more than common acumen and serious thought. The Hebrew is derived from a root, "sharp," that is, calculated to stimulate attention and whet the intellect. Distinct from "fable," in that it teaches not fiction, but fact. Not like the ordinary riddle, designed to puzzle, but to instruct. The "riddle" is here identical with the "parable," only that the former refers to the obscurity, the latter to the likeness of the figure to the thing compared. <div eID="gen20344" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11265"/><div sID="gen20345" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11265"/><hi type="bold">3. eagle--</hi>the king of birds. The literal Hebrew is, "the great eagle." The symbol of the Assyrian supreme god, Nisroch; so applied to "the great king" of Babylon, his vicegerent on earth (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jr 48:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">49:22</reference>). His "wings" are his great forces. Such symbols were familiar to the Jews, who saw them portrayed on the great buildings of Babylon; such as are now seen in the Assyrian remains.<div eID="gen20345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">long-winged--</hi>implying the wide extent of his empire.<div eID="gen20346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">full of feathers--</hi>when they have been renewed after moulting; and so in the full freshness of renovated youth (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.5">Psa 103:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Is 40:31</reference>). Answering to the many peoples which, as tributaries, constituted the strength of Babylon.<div eID="gen20347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">divers colours--</hi>the golden eagle, marked with star-like spots, supposed to be the largest of eagles [Bochart]. Answering to the variety of languages, habits, and costumes of the peoples subject to Babylon.<div eID="gen20348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came unto Lebanon--</hi>continuing the metaphor: as the eagle frequents mountains, not cities. The temple at Jerusalem was called "Lebanon" by the Jews [Eusebius], because its woodwork was wholly of cedars of Lebanon. "The mountain of the Lord's house" (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>). Jerusalem, however, is chiefly meant, the chief seat of civil honor, as Lebanon was of external elevation.<div eID="gen20349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">took the highest branch--</hi>King Jeconiah, then but eighteen years old, and many of the chiefs and people with him (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.8">2Ki 24:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12-2Kgs.24.16">12-16</reference>). The Hebrew for "highest branch" is, properly, the fleece-like tuft at the top of the tree. (So in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.3-Ezek.31.14">Eze 31:3-14</reference>). The cedar, as a tall tree, is the symbol of kingly elevation (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.4.10-Dan.4.12">Da 4:10-12</reference>). <div eID="gen20350" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11266"/><div sID="gen20351" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11266"/><hi type="bold">4. land of traffic ... merchants--</hi>Babylon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.15">2Ki 24:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.16">16</reference>), famous for its transport traffic on the Tigris and Euphrates. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11267"/><div sID="gen20352" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11267"/><hi type="bold">5. seed of the land--</hi>not a foreign production, but one native in the region; a son of the soil, not a foreigner: Zedekiah, uncle of Jehoiachin, of David's family.<div eID="gen20352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in a fruitful field--</hi>literally, a "field of seed"; that is, fit for propagating and continuing the seed of the royal family.<div eID="gen20353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a willow--</hi>derived from a Hebrew root, "to overflow," from its fondness for water (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.4">Is 44:4</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11269"/><div sID="gen20358" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11269"/><hi type="bold">7. another ... eagle--</hi>the king of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.15">Eze 17:15</reference>). The "long-winged" of <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference> is omitted, as Egypt had not such a wide empire and large armies as Babylon.<div eID="gen20358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vine ... bend ... roots towards him--</hi>literally, "thirsted after him with its roots"; expressing the longings after Egypt in the Jewish heart. Zedekiah sought the alliance of Egypt, as though by it he could throw off his dependence on Babylon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.13">2Ch 36:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jr 37:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen20359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20360" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">water it by ... furrows of ... plantation--</hi>that is, in the garden beds (Judea) wherein (the vine) it was planted. Rather, "by" or "out of the furrows." It refers to the waters of Egypt, the Nile being made to water the fields by means of small canals or "furrows"; these waters are the figure of the auxiliary forces wherewith Egypt tried to help Judah. See the same figure, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Is 8:7</reference>. But see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.10">Eze 17:10</reference>, "furrows where it grew." <div eID="gen20360" type="x-p"/>

When the state of Israel shall seem past recovery, Messiah, Jehovah Himself, will unexpectedly appear on the scene as Redeemer of His people (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">Is 63:5</reference>).<div eID="gen20387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ... also--</hi>God opposes Himself to Nebuchadnezzar: "He took of the seed of the land and planted it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.5">5</reference>), so will I, but with better success than he had. The branch he plucked (Zedekiah) and planted, flourished but for a time, to perish at last; I will plant a scion of the same tree, the house of David, to whom the kingdom belongs by an everlasting covenant, and it shall be the shelter of the whole world, and shall be for ever."<div eID="gen20388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">branch--</hi>the peculiar title of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zec 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.6.12">6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Is 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">33:15</reference>).<div eID="gen20389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a tender one--</hi>Zerubbabel never reigned as a universal (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.23">Eze 17:23</reference>) king, nor could the great things mentioned here be said of him, except as a type of Messiah.
